lesson.title: Sprachen: die Sprache, französisch, englisch, spanisch, italienisch
lesson.subtitle: the language names are the country names wearing -isch — and -isch is English's own -ish

hook.title: die Sprache Is What sprechen Leaves Behind
hook.content: die Sprache is the noun made from sprechen — speak's own k→ch twin (Buch/book, Milch/milk). Sprache is literally 'that which is spoken': the talking, and then, by extension, the whole system a people talks with. Now look at the four language names, because they are the country names from the last two lessons wearing a suffix: Frankreich → französisch, Spanien → spanisch, Italien → italienisch, England → englisch. That suffix -isch is the aha of the lesson: it is English's own -ish. Both descend from one Proto-Germanic ending, *-iskaz — so englisch and english are the same word built the same way, and Irish, Scottish and Danish carry the English half of it into the present. Even deutsch wears it: the word from Länder I that became Dutch in English is *þiudiskaz, 'of the people' — the -isk is sitting right there in the oldest member of the family. And when the language stands for itself as a noun, German capitalizes it: Ich spreche Französisch.

footnotes.title: Capital or Lowercase?
footnotes.content: As a noun — the language itself — German capitalizes: Ich spreche Englisch, Ich lerne Französisch. As an adjective in front of a noun it stays lowercase: ein französisches Buch, die französische Sprache. Same word, two costumes — the capital tells you it is the language.

pattern.title: Speaking About Speaking
pattern.content: Four frames. 1. State it: Ich spreche Englisch und Deutsch — the language after sprechen is a capitalized noun. 2. Ask it: Sprechen Sie Spanisch? — formal Sie, verb first, language capitalized. 3. Count it: Wir sprechen drei Sprachen — die Sprache pluralizes to die Sprachen like any die noun. 4. Pair it: England → englisch, Frankreich → französisch, Spanien → spanisch, Italien → italienisch — and the odd one out is Deutschland, whose language deutsch was the original -isch word of all. One warning from the pairs: adverbial uses stay lowercase — Wir essen oft italienisch means eating Italian-style, no noun in sight.
pattern.linguist_note: *-iskaz is one suffix wearing three national costumes: German -isch (englisch, irisch, schottisch), English -ish (English, Irish, Scottish), and Scandinavian -sk (Danish dansk). The sound-shape drifted, the job never changed — 'in the style of'. English uses it natively in its own nationality words and borrowed French -esque alongside; German never stopped building with it.

exercises.prompt: Talking about languages — match each sentence with its reading:
exercises.target_answer: Ich spreche Englisch und Deutsch, Sprechen Sie Spanisch, Die französische Sprache ist schön, Wir essen oft italienisch, Wir sprechen drei Sprachen, Die Schweiz hat vier Sprachen, In Österreich spricht man Deutsch, Die Sprache in der Türkei, Die Sprache in Polen, In Irland spricht man Englisch
exercises.meaning: speak, ask about languages, the language noun, eat Italian-style, count languages
exercises.explanation: Every country name from the last two lessons reappears wearing -isch. The capitalized forms (Englisch, Spanisch) are nouns — the language itself; the lowercase französische and italienisch are adjectives doing describing work.

exercises.prompt: die Sprache is built on one of these verbs — 'that which is spoken'. Which one?
exercises.meaning: die Sprache ← sprechen: the k→ch family (speak)
exercises.explanation: sprechen is speak's k→ch twin, and die Sprache is its noun: what is spoken. sagen means 'to say' — a different verb doing a different job — and trinken and leben have no language business at all.

exercises.prompt: -isch and English -ish are one suffix, *-iskaz. englisch : english :: spanisch : ___
exercises.meaning: spanisch ↔ spanish: the same suffix on the same country stem
exercises.explanation: spanisch and spanish are built identically: the country stem + the one Germanic suffix. English kept *-iskaz in its nationality words (English, Irish, Scottish); German never let it go. The pair is audible the moment you say it aloud.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the question: 'Do you speak English?'
exercises.explanation: Verb first with Sie — the question frame you drilled in the first topic. Englisch is capitalized because it is the noun here; swap in Französisch and the frame holds: Sprechen Sie Französisch?

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'Let us speak German right now'
exercises.meaning: Let us speak German right now

vocab_hints.note: your time-lesson adverb — Komm bitte sofort! Here it pushes the whole sentence: no waiting, switch to German now. Sprechen wir... is the let-us frame: verb first, no question mark needed.

exercises.explanation: Sprechen wir sofort Deutsch — the hortative frame (verb first, wir behind) with sofort doing the urgency and Deutsch capitalized as the noun it is. The bank's other three languages fit the same slot: Sprechen wir sofort Französisch.

summary.outcome: Say which languages you speak, ask Sprechen Sie...?, count die Sprachen, and see -isch as English -ish every time.

use_example.german: Ich spreche Englisch — und ich lerne Französisch.
use_example.english: I speak English — and I am learning French.

summary.takeaway: die Sprache is sprechen's k→ch noun; every language name is a country name + -isch; -isch and -ish are one suffix (*-iskaz); language nouns are capitalized: Ich spreche Französisch.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the five jobs a first conversation needs — der Arzt, der Bäcker, der Verkäufer, der Polizist, der Schüler.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Sprachen: die Sprache, französisch, englisch, spanisch, italienisch (Let us speak German right now):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Sprechen wir sofort Deutsch" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Sprachen: die Sprache, französisch, englisch, spanisch, italienisch without relying on short-term echo.

sprache.context_phrase: Die Sprache ist schwer zu lernen.
sprache.context_translation: The language is hard to learn.
sprache.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sprāhha, Proto-West Germanic *sprāku, the twin of English speech; the k to ch velar shift links both to the sprechen and speak family. [wiktionary]

französisch.etymology_derivation: From Old French francois plus the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; both trace back to the Franks, whence also English frank. [wiktionary]

englisch.etymology_derivation: From England plus the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the page itself names English English as the cognate, so this is the same word. [wiktionary]

spanisch.etymology_derivation: Spanien + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Spanish. [wiktionary]

italienisch.etymology_derivation: Italien + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Italian. [wiktionary]

schweiz.etymology_derivation: die Schweiz is named after Schwyz, the canton the country takes its name from. [wiktionary]

österreich.etymology_derivation: Old element for "east" + rīhhi "realm" — the eastern realm (Reich ↔ rich). [wiktionary]

türkei.context_phrase: Der Urlaub war in der Türkei.
türkei.etymology_derivation: Land of the Turks: from Medieval Latin Turcia, influenced by Türke "Turk". [wiktionary]

polen.etymology_derivation: Middle High German Polen, plural of Pole — land of the Poles. [wiktionary]

irland.etymology_derivation: The same name as English Ireland — land of the Irish, shared proper name. [wiktionary]

sofort.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Middle Low German so vōrt — literally 'so forth', mirroring the English phrase. [wiktionary]

deutsch.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz, of the people, built on *þeudō, people; the very same word as English Dutch, with Latin theodiscus and Teutonic sharing the root. [wiktionary]

deutschland.etymology_derivation: diutsch "of the people" + lant "land" — compound: land of the people. [wiktionary]

frankreich.etymology_derivation: Franke "Frank" + Reich "realm" — realm of the Franks. [wiktionary]

england.etymology_derivation: From Old English Engla land — land of the Angles. [wiktionary]

spanien.etymology_derivation: The same Latin name Hispania that English Spain descends from, via Old High German Spānia. [wiktionary]

italien.etymology_derivation: The same Latin name Italia as English Italy; shared proper name, no sound shift to fake. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
